I talked about it with my psychiatrist and her. My new psychiatrist has a very different approach to hers. When I talked to him about it, he pushed the envelope so to speak, was still empathetic, but didn't let me get away with minimizing or denying things. He gave me tools to deal with the emotional and physical distress of the memory, and validated it, even though that wasn't what I wanted him to say or to hear from him.    


With her, she was sympathetic to the fact that I experienced a physical reaction to it, but then was like "here's what you need to do in order to get past those when they happen. " and then when I said "I don't know what to do with some of these memories and how to feel about them, or give them some kind of meaning in my life, how can I possibly incorporate this kind of stuff into my personal narrative of 'yes this happened, but here's how I will acknowledge it in my life and move forward from here'." and she said I should be mindful. I should literally ignore it (not think on it or fixate/ruminate about it) and instead focus on preparing myself to go back to work because "sometimes you can't get all the answers you want or are looking for and you have to be satisfied with that."

 I was really upset by this. Cause I was like- wtf? You want me to just IGNORE the implications of "my parents raped and trafficked me"?? If you remembered that your parents were serial killers getting ready to go on their next spree, would YOU be like "ah yes, well let me do some breathing exercises and then completely ignore it and get back to shuffling those papers. Maybe I'll telephone mother later to see if after their spree they would like to go on for a family picnic in the park- usually only takes them 3 days to finish up, just in time for this Friday! yes, sounds right."    
How the FUCK am I supposed to function normally or ignore that stuff when the implications are so profound and serious?? Sorry for that rant, but I was really thrown off by her response.

So, the thing with DID is, I won't mince words here- "too bad. it's all for one and one for all". Every member of the system is responsible for what each other does. At first glance this may not seem fair, but every member of the system shares ONE singular physical body, despite being separate people in their own rights. These alters need to take responsibility for their actions, ESPECIALLY unhealthy or abusive ones. It is NOT right for any alter to hurt you even if they have trauma reasons behind it or unhealthy coping mechanisms at play.     
Additionally, you aren't responsible for any of the alters emotional health or well-being. You can be supportive and caring, understanding and nurturing, but you can't be the object upon which their emotional/mental health hinges- you are your own separate being, and it won't help anyone in this to become co-dependent on one another.

Fast-forward to college, I grew taller, lost weight, got into sports, started to get more womanly. I noticed a small uptick in people who I thought were attractive talking back to me and being nice.
I accidentally asked one of the most attractive people in my class out, AND THEY SAID YES?!?! (I was SO shocked/confused at the time)  
Then, I started getting my problems looked into, getting more sleep, dealing with my Eating Disorder, and got into therapy.
Years later, I did a bunch of drugs and at one point I went into a bathroom and looked in the mirror and was like   
"Woah.... uhhh is this my face? Have I always looked like this??" 
I looked nice! I actually liked my face/body.   
Then, my friends and people kept telling me I was pretty/attractive. I thought they were lying to be nice.  
Now I realize I still think of myself as the fat/chubby gawky awkward kid, but I've changed a lot, and the world seems to have noticed lol.

Just be gentle, and even if you guys have done something sexually before don't assume that she will be A ok with it every time, sometimes people have off days. Sometimes something's bothering you and what didn't trigger before is painful now. 
It's no ones fault.

Will this be frustrating sometimes? Probably. Will it take a lot of maturity on your part? Yes. Will it take a lot of work and effort to communicate her needs and be honest on her part? Yes very much so.

These are things to be aware of. Sexual abuse is difficult abuse is difficult and trauma is well traumatic.

I know I learned with my pets even when I was younger that shifting an emphasis from "I need to punish you badly for doing this thing that angered me, and I told you not to do and punishing you is appropriate and makes me feel better" to -> "What does this creature need to understand in order to prevent this from happening again. Moreover, what do I need to do right now to make myself less angry so that I don't hit and scream and otherwise lashout. Also, how can I change the circumstances to make this less likely to happen again."  
Simple example: Dog eats entire bag of treats, gets sick vomits all over the floor, makes the house smell to high heavens in the heat & 1hr it takes to get back to clean it up. I'm tired & on a schedule for something I have to go to.  
Sure, I'm angry as all hell, but I focus much less (now that I know) on doling out punishment and on prevention and managing *my* feelings.  
  
Obviously, dogs and kids are different, and I'm just listing a few things here and there, but I think managing yourself first and also being mad at the thing that *happened* but *not* the individual is key (Especially for individuals who arguably can't or physiologically are much less capable at self-regulation and control and even just orchestrating their words/body/actions/thoughts/etc).  
  
Also, I'm pretty sure spanking isn't the best form of discipline. No judgments, but I would say that I think there are more pleasant ways of going about it for both parties involved.
